previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Meléndez, a man with a history of dilated cardiomyopathy, systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and chronic alcohol use, was admitted after being assaulted and reporting chest pain near his defibrillator, along with episodes of hematemesis. He was initially managed in the MICU for alcohol withdrawal, receiving benzodiazepines, and was found to have elevated lactate likely due to withdrawal. His chest pain was determined to be musculoskeletal, with no device damage or myocardial infarction. The hematemesis was attributed to a possible Mallory-Weiss tear or gastritis, and he was treated with a proton pump inhibitor. He remained stable, tolerated a regular diet, and was restarted on anticoagulation. He expressed interest in sobriety but declined medications and discharge paperwork at discharge. He was discharged home with follow-up recommendations.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ yoM with h/o HTN, Afib, dilated CMP, systolic CHF (EF 25% in 
___, STEMI ___ s/p cardiac catherization, VT s/p AICD, PE 
in ___ s/p 6 months of enoxaparin, who presented with report 
of syncope and hematemesis.

# Syncope: He reported two episodes of syncope with ICD firing 
prior to admission.  His story was inconsistent and he has 
reported multiple times that his ICD has fired but it has never 
has fired per ICD interrogations.  He was admitted from the ED 
as he met ___ syncope criteria.  He was monitored on 
telemetry throughout admission and had one 5 beat run of VT with 
no symptoms and no other abnormalities. EP was consulted and 
case was discussed with EP attending Dr. ___ stated that he 
did not feel it was indicated to interrogate his ICD again as he 
keeps claiming it is shocking him when it is not.  He 
recommended outpatient follow-up.  It is expected that he may 
have short runs of VT given his low EF but that this is unlikely 
to cause syncope.  He had orthostatics checked which were 
negative.  He had no syncope during admission and was walking 
around wihtout difficulty.  Given his inconsistent story and his 
lack of objective evidence of any abnormality, it was felt that 
his presentation may have been due to secondary gain given his 
social situation.

# Hematemesis: He reported multiple episodes of vomiting blood 
on presentation.  He was reportedly guaiac positive in the ED 
per the ED signout, although per the attending note he was 
guaiac negative.  He was seen by the GI team here but given his 
inconsistent history and his lack of any objective evidence of 
hematemesis with completely stable Hct, an EGD was not felt to 
be indicated.  He was treated with a BID PPI.  A H pylori stool 
Ag is pending given his history.  He may have some 
alcohol-related gastritis and should continue a PPI.  He should 
not be readmitted for hematemesis without objective evidence of 
GI bleeding.

# Chest pain: He has a chronic chest pain syndrome as well as 
pain over his ICD after a recent assault.  He continued to 
complain of chest pain and ECG was unchanged from recent 
admission (he did have some TWI which were new on last 
admission, please see prior ___ summary).  He also reported no 
relief with SL nitro prior to admission.  He was ruled out for 
MI and monitored on telemetry.

# H/o HTN, afib, dilated CMP, systolic CHF (EF 25% in ___, 
STEMI ___ s/p cardiac catherization, VT s/p AICD, PE in 
___ s/p 6 months of enoxaparin: He appeared euvolemic on exam 
and was continued on metoprolol and losartan.  Aspirin and 
pradaxa were initially held but restarted prior to discharge.

# Etoh abuse: Unfortunately the ED did not send an alcohol level 
on presentation and unable to be added on.  Unclear if he drank 
alcohol since last admission but he did not have signs of 
withdrawal.  He was seen by social work during this admission.

TRANSITIONAL ISSUES:
- There was significant concern for secondary gain this 
admission as he complained of syncope with ICD shocks, 
hematemesis, chest pain, and multiple other symptoms without any 
objective evidence of abnormality.  He was encouraged to 
follow-up with his outpatient providers, including our device 
clinic, for outpatient interrogation of his ICD.  Unfortunately 
he does have a strong medical history, especially a cardiac 
history, but he did not have any consistent complaints and his 
story changed so often that it is quite difficult to tell 
secondary gain from true pathology in this gentleman.  Over the 
last two admissions, he has had many serious complaints with a 
negative workup and would base admission decisions and clinical 
workup on objective evidence in the future.
